They did not survey first the area for signs and the usual location of rip currents (i.e. channel or gaps along the shore). You do not swim when engulfed by a rip current, one should float and relax. Panic and ignorance on their part did it. you do not swim because you shall only get tired and exhausted. No real preparation and safety preparation for this activity. The lifeguard of the resort should know about the danger signs of incipient rip currents. water activities in the ocean should mandate wearing of life vests. Take time to read this‼️‼️I really feel it was Rene who tried to save Divine. He grew up in Agusan, and according to his grandmother, he knows how to swim. So here’s what likely happened: when the rip current struck, panic set in fast — both ended up swallowing water. Meanwhile, Divine's mother confirmed her son does not know how to swim at all. She surely panicked immediately, and Rene went to help him — so they ended up together in the water.
In that kind of crisis, you lose your sense of what to do — it’s common that when someone is struggling, they instinctively climb or lean on whoever is near them, just to stay above water and breathe. That’s probably exactly what happened: in her panic, Divine ended up resting his whole weight on top of Rene. Since Divine is heavier, it dragged him down. This also matches what was seen when they were recovered — Rene was already unresponsive/unstable, while Divine still had a pulse. Rene likely sank first because of the extra weight pressing him down while both were fighting the current.

text:
After hearing the accounts of what happened, it sounds like this was a tragic accident but one that may have been largely preventable. It is heartbreaking that two lives were lost. ADMU and its basketball coaching and management team should be held accountable because the incident occurred during an official training activity under their supervision.

Another concerning detail, as a healthcare professional, is the report that CPR may have been delayed or interrupted. I am trying to understand why transport would be prioritized over immediate, continuous life-saving efforts given that the nearest hospital is reportedly almost an hour away. High-quality, uninterrupted CPR is one of the most critical factors in resuscitating a drowning victim and it should be continued during transport when possible. Even in the hospital, when a patient codes during transport, we continue CPR without delay. We either climb on the bed or work alongside it while moving the patient.

EVERY MINUTE MATTERS. It is difficult to ignore the feeling that a significant amount of precious time may have been lost in the response.


RIP RENE AND DIVINE 🙏🏻🕊️

To the rest of the ADMU players, I hope you find peace and strength as you recover from this tragedy. May you be surrounded with support as you process everything that has happened.

text:
This episode brought back a memory from Saud Beach in Pagudpud.

My sister and I got caught in a rip current years ago.

We both knew how to swim. It didn’t matter.

We were carried farther and farther from shore. We shouted and waved for help, but the wind was so strong nobody seemed to hear us.

Eventually we were just treading water, exhausted. My sister was begging me to help her, but I was struggling just to keep myself afloat.

I remember thinking, “Lord, is this really how I die?”

Then I heard my mom’s voice in my head:

“Float like a dead man.”

So I did.

Eventually I was carried back to shore, far from where we started. I looked back and saw my sister still out there.

I shouted, “Float like a dead man!”

She heard me.

A little later, she made it back too.

Afterward, we sat side by side near the showers and didn’t say a word for the longest time.

If there’s one thing I’d tell people, it’s this: learn to swim, respect the sea, and never attempt a rescue without a flotation device.

video_title: Ateneo de Manila Blue Eagles Kieffer Alas and Sam Reyes speak up
text:
I can still remember that tragic day as if it happened yesterday, and even now, the pain of it stays with me.
We were at Buguey Beach with two of our staff members. It was supposed to be a simple stopover, just a chance to relax for a while. One of our staff decided to go into the water. Three stayed on the shore , watching him. He was only about a meter away from the children playing near the sand, and from where I stood, the water looked shallow, no more than knee-deep.
Then everything changed in an instant.
A large wave suddenly hit him. I heard him call out for help, and before we could react, another wave came. He tried a third time to jump up and call for help, but after that, we could no longer see him. The waves just kept coming.
We immediately called for the lifeguard, but he was unable to reach him in time. Rescuers from the MDRRMO arrived quickly with a life buoy and did everything they could, but they could not save him. Divers from Santa Ana, Cagayan were also called, but they were nearly two hours away. By then, what started as a rescue effort had sadly became a retrieval operation.
His body was recovered the following day.

One moment we were all together, and the next, he was gone. The next hard thing is to call his family hoping what just happened was a nightmare..

For a long time, I carried so many questions and so much guilt. I kept wondering if there was something more I could have done. Even today, whenever I hear about similar incidents, it brings me right back to that day and the heartbreak we experienced.
It is a pain I would never wish on anyone.

text: Truth be told, there is really nothing strange about the team-building exercises that the players were asked to do. They are meant to build camaraderie and stamina. The team has been in this place several times before, although some of the players were new to the experience. This is the unpredictability of the place and the sea. The Aurora province is facing the Pacific ocean where the continental shelf is narrow and therefore more susceptible to wave changes. The locals have a belief that some places have a tendency to collect lives from the unsuspecting - buwis buhay. This happens even in shallow rivers and strangely even good swimmers have fallen victims. Surely this may be a form of superstitious belief, but this kind of situation has happened so many times before. Often the victims are  new to the place. The force that caught the victims is rip current. And its impact is really powerful and its impact is magnified when the affected panics. The fact is the victims really don't know the place that they thought they knew. And even if they knew the place, the place and the situation were really changing. The team didn't think the place was risky, but it was. Surely, more safety measures could have been put in place, but when you are at the moment you tend to be overwhelmed. Surely no one wanted this to happen. But lessons are learned after the fact. We may advice people not to underestimate the force of nature, but there will always be risk takers and I doubt that this will not happen again to some other people.

@strainedsatirePh  Nagsalita kasi binash? Ganun? Eh ang labo niyo naman.

Noong tahimik pa sila, puro kayo “SPEAK UP!” at “Bakit walang nagsasalita?” Ngayong nagsalita na, sasabihin niyo naman, “Nagsalita lang kasi na-bash.” So ano ba talaga? Gusto niyo ba silang magsalita, o gusto niyo lang marinig yung gusto niyong marinig?

Masyado kayong obsessed sa sarili ninyong narratives. Ayan na nga, nagsalita na. Pero dahil hindi pasok sa kwentong ginawa niyo sa utak niyo, ayaw niyo pa rin paniwalaan. Kasi ang gusto niyo, validation. Hindi katotohanan.

And please, stop acting like these kids owe you a perfect timeline and a perfect response after experiencing something traumatic. Hindi sila robots. Hindi sila PR team. Mga bata rin silang dumaan sa isang trahedya.

At bakit ba sobrang gigil na gigil kayong sisihin ang mga estudyante? Sila na nga ’yung muntik mamatay, sila pa ang ginagawang kontrabida? Make it make sense.

Kung may dapat panagutin dito, hindi ’yung mga batang halos hindi na makabalik nang buhay. Panagutin niyo ’yung mga taong may responsibilidad sa kanila. Panagutin niyo ang coaching staff. Panagutin niyo ang university. Kasi sila ang may authority. Sila ang adults. Sila ang may obligasyon na siguraduhing ligtas ang mga batang ipinagkatiwala sa kanila.

At sana, bago kayo magpakalat ng kung anu-anong conclusions, matuto muna kayong mag-fact check. Hindi porket marami kayong opinion, tama na kayo. Hindi porket maingay kayo, may sense na kayo.

And may Rene and Divine rest in peace. Fly high, our beloved MVPs. 🕊️🤍

After listening to the podcast interview with Sam and Kiefer, it appears that several players experienced situations that could have become life-threatening. If the coaches were already aware of the dangers of rip currents and the risks associated with the area, it is reasonable to ask whether enough precautions were taken from the very beginning.

One important question is whether previous activities in the same location created a false sense of security simply because no one had been seriously harmed before. Just because a dangerous situation did not result in tragedy in the past does not mean the risk was not there. Safety should never depend on luck.

There should have been clear safety guidelines, risk assessments, and emergency procedures in place before the activity began. Considering that there were multiple coaches and staff members involved, supervision and safety monitoring should have been a top priority. Experienced coaches, especially those with many years of leadership, are expected to recognize potential dangers and take the necessary steps to protect their athletes.

It is difficult to imagine that any coach would want to see their players placed in life-threatening situations. However, when a tragedy occurs, it is important to examine whether proper decisions were made and whether safety measures were adequate.

Questions may also be raised about whether there were enough personnel assigned to monitor the activity and whether emergency responders and medical staff had the training, equipment, and knowledge needed to handle a drowning emergency effectively. In critical situations, every minute and every decision can make a difference.

As for the teammates, it is important to remember that many of them were reportedly struggling in the same dangerous conditions. During moments of fear, panic, and survival, people may not immediately realize who is missing. The fact that some players remembered Divine may be because they had spent more time with him through games and team activities. Nevertheless, the loss of a teammate is heartbreaking for everyone involved. Kawawang Rene dahil bago lang sya walang nakaalala sa knya na nawawala na din sya sa dami nila .😭

What happened is truly tragic. The families of Rene and Divine deserve transparency, timely communication, and respect. Accountability is important because a simple apology alone cannot answer all the questions surrounding the incident. A thorough and independent investigation is necessary to determine what happened, identify any failures, and ensure that similar tragedies can be prevented in the future.

This situation serves as a reminder to all schools, coaches, and sports organizations that athlete safety must always come first. Leadership is not only measured by victories and achievements but also by the responsibility to protect the lives and well-being of those entrusted to their care.

They also shouldn’t have been complacent just because the water was said to be “mababaw.” This wasn’t a controlled swimming pool where conditions stay the same. It was open water where currents, uneven depths, and changing conditions can make the situation dangerous very quickly.

Accidents can happen but when there are known risks and previous warning signs, it’s reasonable to ask whether enough was done to keep the players safe.

text:
Grabe kawawa lahat ng mga student athletes nato... Im watching their interview now. Ang negligent ng nagplano na mag watee activity sa open water na alam na palang may rip current ni Coach Tab Baldwin dun. So actually he risked all these athletes' lives. And totoo talaga pag may rip current pwede ka madala sa malayo and mag panic kahit marunong ka mag swim and kahit na galing ka lang sa mababaw. 

And a kwento ng mga bata nato, it's so obvious walang life guards nearby! 

Nakawitness nako ng ganito sa la union year 2022 holy week. Friday ata yun or saturday.  Nasa knee-deep lang yung mga taong tinangay ng current na around 3-5feet away from me lang. And seconds lang din nasa malayo na sila and bigla na lang ako nakarinig sigawan. Ako nasa mga ankle deep lang ako kasi yung waves pag nadating nalagpas ulo kahit nasa around 2 feet lang ako away from buhangin na walang water. Pero nararamdaman ko yung sand sa ilalim lumalalim parang naghihila yung water. Ayun may 5 tinangay. May mga surfer dun na may sirf board na sila yung nagsagip sa mga tao ang dami ng surfers pero even sila nag panic. Nakita ko yung isa na naligtas ang dami sinuka dami nainom water. And may isa hindi na nakita ilang oras na di pa din nakita yung 16yo. 

Grabe ang traumatic nun. Prior to that nag surfing lesson eme eme pa ako 1hour tinatangay din ako sa lagpas tao pero nakakabit sa paa ko surfboard pero nakakapanic pa din makabalik sa surf board kasi ang lakas alon. So sabi ko sa instructor ko ok nako naka 1 hour na din. Di ko pa alam nun na pwede matangay ng rip current. 

Kaya now trauma nako sa lahat ng beach . hanggang dun lang ako lagi sa konting nababasa lang paa ko lolz.

And locals sa la union told me madami talaga nalulinod dun di lang narereport. Then i told a friend na natangay din sya ng rio current sa baler naman mabuti naka attacj din sya sa surf board. At naligtas ng mga surfers. At sabi din sa kanya madami din daw nalulinod dun di lang nababalita.

ofc there should be no pressure on any survivor to speak if they're not ready. trauma takes time to process and everyone heals differently. but whenever they are ready, their stories could help the families of those who were lost better understand what happened that day and perhaps give them some measure of closure.

My heart goes out to the families and everyone affected.

Assess d situation - where is d direction of d  current going or pulling you away.
 Pray, stay calm, dont panic and save your breath. 
Wag mong aawayin yung tubig when it pulls you down or away. 
After it had passed, hopefully makaahon ka pag nasa malalim ka or kung napalayo... makaswim pabalik

While watching this, I honestly couldn’t stop crying. It keeps making my mind spiral with so many “why’s,” and the feeling is just so heavy. Grabe, ang bigat sa dibdib habang pinapanood ko. There’s this kind of pain that just sits with you, the type that doesn’t go away even after the video ends. The hurt of losing someone in a situation like this is already unbearable, but what makes it even heavier is the feeling that others are being dragged into it or being blamed along the way. It feels unfair, confusing, and emotionally exhausting at the same time.

Sa 35:41, it really stands out when Sam said, “kung di po ako umalis dito mamatay nadin po ako dito.” It raises so many uncomfortable questions about what was really known and what wasn’t being fully explained. And certain details not being addressed in formal settings like CIDG and NBI, but appearing in a podcast instead, just makes everything feel more confusing and incomplete.

The whole 1 hour and 30 minutes felt like it went on without truly addressing accountability, justice, or liability in a clear and direct way. Instead of answers, it leaves gaps. Instead of clarity, it leaves silence. And that silence feels heavier than anything else.This is not about blaming the players involved. Pero sana, kung ano man talaga yung totoo, sabihin na lang nang buo at malinaw. People deserve transparency, especially when the situation already involves loss, confusion, and pain. Hindi yung pilit na nagiging vague yung mga sagot, kasi mas lalo lang nitong pinapahirap para sa lahat na maintindihan kung ano talaga yung nangyari.

At the end of it all, what stays is grief, confusion, and frustration. The pain of loss, the weight of unanswered questions, and the hope that truth will be fully told, without omission or distortion, so that people can finally find some clarity and closure.

Negligence! 

Even if they had been doing this activity for the past 10 years, that does not automatically make it safe. If the area is known for strong waves, rip currents, or dangerous open-water conditions, then continuing to bring students there is like saying, “Let’s see if fire can actually burn.”

That is not experience. That is complacency. At some point, if you keep ignoring obvious risks, it stops looking like an accident and starts looking like a failure of basic judgment. As if the coaching staff have a foresight of a potato.

I feel bad for all the students involved because the adults failed them. If you are bringing young people into the freaking Pacific Ocean, there should have been proper safeguards: lifeguards on standby, flotation devices, rescue boats or personnel nearby, emergency medical support, and a clear rescue plan. May briefing kayo about ripcurrents tapos rescue plan at floatters wala?

This is what makes it so painful. It feels preventable.

These are still kids. Realistically, many students will just follow instructions, trust the adults, and go with the flow. They may not feel comfortable questioning a coach, a school authority, or a group activity, especially in a culture where speaking up can easily be seen as being difficult.

That is why adult responsibility matters even more.

I also wonder if parents were clearly informed about the exact activities planned. If more parents had known the full details, maybe more people would have asked the right questions: Is this safe? What are the risks? Are there lifeguards? Are there flotation devices? What happens if someone gets swept away?

Sometimes, more eyes mean more foresight. And in this case, that kind of foresight could have mattered.

And yes, it is also sad to see other students being bashed, because they are also traumatized.

But the pain of Rene and Divine’s families should not be minimized either. Two young lives were lost. If the typical filipino is mad about this news, ano pa yung mga bata na nakita na inaahon yung teammates nila? 

It's exhausting to see this news on my fyp, but I hope we don't forget it and really push for accountability.

oh my gosh guys... can we please stop attacking those who survived?

i understand the anger. i understand the grief. i understand wanting answers. we all want to know what happened. we all wish things had turned out differently. 

but imagine being one of the people who survived. imagine watching your teammates disappear before your eyes. imagine realizing that no matter what you did, you couldn't save everyone. imagine carrying that memory for the rest of your life. and now imagine opening social media only to see strangers blaming you for surviving.

as a psych student, one thing i've learned is not everyone can immediately speak up after experiencing something horrifying. some people cry. some people go silent. some people replay the incident in their heads over and over again, trying to make sense of it. trauma doesn't come with a script y'all.

the fact that they did not speak publicly right away does not mean they didn't care. it does not mean they are hiding something. it does not mean they are unaffected. 

remember that they have lost teammates, friends, people they trained with, laughed with, and spent countless hours with. the grief we feel from afar is heartbreaking enough. now imagine the grief of those who were actually there.

before we judge their silence, let's remember that survival itself can be traumatic. they are victims of this tragedy too.

let's seek the truth, yes. let's ask questions, yes. but please! pleaseee... let's not forget our humanity in the process.

video_title: Ateneo de Manila Blue Eagles Kieffer Alas and Sam Reyes speak up
text:
Some of you ask, "Why only speak now?" as if people who witnessed a traumatic event are expected to hold a press conference the next day. They were there. They lost someone they cared about. Shock, grief, guilt, and trauma can affect how and when a person is able to share their experience. A delayed statement is not evidence of foul play. Stop treating normal human responses to trauma as suspicious simply because they don't fit the timeline you've created in your heads.

I'm not defending negligence or saying the school shouldn't be held accountable. But have some compassion for the people who were there too. They were placed in the same dangerous situation, witnessed something traumatic, and lost their teammates. We can ask difficult questions without dehumanizing those who are grieving.

These were people who nearly lost their lives. They thought it might be their last moment. And yet here we are, with others saying things like “sana sila na lang” or even sending threats. How low can it get? Do you really think you know everyone’s perspective? Do you think you’re in a position to judge every intention and every action from behind a screen?

Comments saying things like "sana si _ na lang."???? That's not seeking accountability anymore—that's cruelty.

The surviving players are speaking up now, and people still say, "sabihin niyo kasi yung totoo." But what truth are you willing to accept if you've already decided what you want to hear? It seems like unless their statements match the narrative people have built in their heads, they'll never be believed anyway.

You can demand accountability without wishing death on others or treating survivors like they have to earn your empathy.

“Scripted”? On what basis? Because it doesn’t fit the story you already decided to believe? That’s exactly the problem—people form conclusions first, then force everything they see to match it, even without verified information.

If there are failures in handling this situation, then yes, those should be addressed at the institutional level, the school, the coaches, the system. But the way some people are turning this into speculation, harassment, and misinformation is not helping anyone.

At the very least, use common sense. Think critically. Please, use your judgment and don’t be easily misled by narratives that haven’t been verified.

And regardless of whether this was an accident or not, accountability should still be taken seriously. Someone still has to be held responsible for what led to this.

text: @limarg.official228  Post-Mortem Marks (Livor Mortis)If a drowning is fatal, the body will naturally develop marks that closely mimic bruises.After the heart stops, gravity pulls blood down to the lowest parts of the body, a process called livor mortis.Because a drowning victim typically floats or rests in a face-down (prone) position with limbs hanging downward, blood heavily pools in the face, neck, upper torso, hands, and feet.This creates dark red, blue, or purple skin discolorations that can easily be mistaken for physical bruising by an untrained eye.
